chapter.title: Food Industry Residues and Prepared Animal Feed

page.h1: HTS Chapter 23: Food Industry Residues and Prepared Animal Feed — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Chapter 23 Export Rules: Schedule B, APHIS Certificates for Pet Food & Feed, Phytosanitary Certificates
seo.shortDescription: What U.S. exporters of soybean meal, DDGS, pet food and animal feed must do before shipping, which USDA and FDA certificates buyers ask for, and how to pay less abroad.
keywords: FDA certificate of free sale animal feed

intro: For most of this chapter the U.S. side is routine: find the Schedule B number, screen the buyer and file the export in AES. No Chapter 23 good needs a Commerce export licence in the ordinary case. What adds work is the certificates that only a U.S. agency can issue and that most buyers ask for: an **APHIS-endorsed health certificate** for pet food and anything made from animal material, often from a plant APHIS has inspected for that country; a **phytosanitary certificate** for soybean meal, DDGS and other plant-based feed when the buyer’s plant-quarantine rules require one; and **FDA export certificates** for feed and pet food. Official USDA inspection and weighing of meal and DDGS is voluntary but often written into the sales contract.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Each product has its own Schedule B line: soybean meal is 2304.00.0000; distillers’ dried grains (DDGS) are 2303.30.0000 ("brewing or distilling dregs and waste"); corn gluten feed and corn gluten meal are 2303.10.0010 and 2303.10.0020; dog and cat food for retail sale is 2309.10.0000; and prepared livestock and poultry feeds are split by animal under 2309.90.10xx.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Chapter 23 goods are EAR99: no Export Control Classification Number covers feed, oilseed meal or pet food, so no Commerce licence is needed in the ordinary case. A licence can still be required for a sanctioned destination or a prohibited end user.

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: Bulk soybean meal and DDGS cargoes are far above the $2,500-per-Schedule-B-number threshold, and even one container of pet food usually is, so an AES filing is the norm for this chapter.

rules.title: Health certificate for pet food and animal-origin feed: when the buyer’s country requires one, APHIS endorses an export certificate for pet food and treats, meat-and-bone meal, fishmeal and feeds containing animal ingredients, checked against that country’s requirements. Many countries (the EU, China, Korea and Canada among them) accept product only from a facility APHIS has inspected for that country. APHIS’s animal product export pages list the requirements and certificates country by country; the service is set up under 9 CFR Part 156.

citations.label: APHIS: Animal product exports (requirements by country)
APHIS: Export animal products to Canada (pet food certificate)
9 CFR Part 156 (voluntary inspection and certification service)

rules.title: Phytosanitary certificate for plant-based feed: the U.S. does not require one, but many buyers’ plant-quarantine authorities do for soybean meal, DDGS, bran, beet pulp and other plant-origin feed. An authorized certification official inspects the lot and issues the certificate through APHIS’s PCIT system.

citations.label: APHIS: Plant and plant product export certificates

rules.title: FDA export certificates for feed and pet food: many buyers ask for an FDA certificate (a Certificate of Free Sale or Certificate to Foreign Government for animal food that can be sold in the U.S., or a Certificate of Exportability for animal food made only for export). CVM issues them electronically through its eCATS portal. Animal food that does not meet U.S. requirements can be exported only if it meets the buyer’s specifications and law, with records kept under 21 CFR 1.101.

citations.label: FDA: Exporting animal feed and animal drugs
FDA: Apply for animal food and drug export certificates (CVM eCATS)

rules.title: Official inspection and weighing of meal and DDGS: unlike whole grain and soybeans, processed commodities such as soybean meal, DDGS and corn gluten are not under the Grain Standards Act’s mandatory export inspection. FGIS inspects and weighs them on request under the Agricultural Marketing Act, and many sales contracts and buyers’ import rules call for its official certificate.

citations.label: USDA AMS: Federal Grain Inspection Service
7 CFR Part 868 (inspection of processed and graded commodities)

groups.label: Meat & fish meal
groups.note: Animal-origin meals need an APHIS-endorsed certificate wherever the buyer requires one, and several countries limit or ban meal made from ruminants, so check the APHIS country page before quoting.

groups.label: Bran & milling residues
groups.note: Bran and milling residues are plant-origin feed: a phytosanitary certificate when the buyer requires one; otherwise routine.

groups.label: Starch residues, beet pulp & distillers' grains
groups.note: DDGS and corn gluten feed and meal usually ship with a phytosanitary certificate and an FGIS certificate of quality and weight, as the contract or the buyer requires.

groups.label: Soybean meal
groups.note: Soybean meal is the chapter’s biggest export: FGIS inspection and weighing on request and a phytosanitary certificate where the buyer requires one are the usual extras.

groups.label: Acorns, citrus pulp & other plant feed
Pet food & prepared animal feed
groups.note: Pet food and prepared feed carry the most paperwork: an APHIS-endorsed certificate (often from a plant APHIS has inspected for that country) when they contain animal ingredients, and an FDA certificate when the buyer asks for one.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Use the EU’s duty-free quota for U.S. pet food and feed
savings.saves: The EU duty on certain dog and cat food and feed preparations (9.6%, or €23–102 per tonne) on up to 40,000 tonnes a year of U.S. goods.
savings.appliesTo: U.S.-origin goods under CN 2309 10 51, 2309 10 90, 2309 90 31, 2309 90 41 and 2309 90 96, imported into the EU from July 1, 2026, in 12-month quota periods.
savings.document: The EU importer claims quota order number 09.9007 in its customs declaration; the goods must be of U.S. origin under the EU’s non-preferential origin rules.
savings.caveat: The quota is shared by all EU importers of U.S. goods and is managed first come, first served; once it is used up, the normal EU rate applies until the next period.

savings.title: Have the Chinese buyer apply for an exclusion from China’s 2018–19 counter-tariffs
savings.saves: China’s older counter-tariffs (5–10% on listed feed and pet-food lines) on top of its normal rate and today’s 10% extra tariff.
savings.appliesTo: Chapter 23 lines on China’s 2018–19 counter-tariff lists, such as prepared animal feed (2309.90), canned dog and cat food (2309.10.10), meat-and-bone meal, cereal bran and beet pulp.
savings.document: An exclusion application by the Chinese importer through China’s Tariff Commission exclusion process.
savings.caveat: The exclusions run only to December 31, 2026 under the November 2025 U.S.–China deal, and they do not lift China’s 10% extra tariff on all U.S. goods or its anti-dumping and countervailing duties on DDGS.

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
